title: Newbigin's return
hook: a missionary to India returns to Britain and sees the West as a mission field too

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pentecostal theology: the Spirit's power, given for a purpose. Your line was power to witness. Who heard something good and true from you? Day one thousand two hundred eighty-one.

A young minister sits in South India, saying Tamil words aloud until they stick. He has sailed out from Britain as a missionary of the Church of Scotland, and he stays for years. He preaches in villages, and becomes a bishop in the Church of South India. Then, near the end of his working life, he comes home to Britain. And home looks strange to him. Thinner congregations. A culture that once called itself Christian, now living by other stories. Lesslie Newbigin looked hard at his own country and said it plainly: the West is a mission field too. Today, Newbigin's return, and the last day of this week.
screen: `THE WEST IS A MISSION FIELD TOO.`

segments.voice: A missionary has to learn to see a culture from outside: what its people take for granted, what stories they live by, what they'd never think to question. Newbigin had done that for years in India. Back in Britain, he turned the same eyes on his own culture. He saw that the modern West had its own unquestioned beliefs, like any culture, and he thought Christians there had made too much peace with them without noticing. So he asked the missionary's question at home: how does the gospel sound here, to these neighbors? His answer had a surprising focus. Not mainly big campaigns. The local congregation. He wrote that a congregation actually living the gospel, in its worship, its care for neighbors and its life together, is how people come to understand the gospel at all. In John's Gospel, the risen Jesus says to his disciples: "as my Father hath sent me, even so send I you." Newbigin drew no line there between those who go far away and those who stay. For him, every disciple is sent, and home is where the sending starts. This week has walked through a house of many rooms. Rahner: mystic in the ordinary. Schmemann: the world as sacrament. Gutiérrez: from below. Cone: the cross stands with them. Women's voices: her story too. Pentecostals: power to witness. And Newbigin, seeing his own front door with fresh eyes.

Here's the practice: see your home with fresh eyes. Settle, and breathe. Picture the street where you live, or the building, or the town. Now look at it the way a newcomer would, someone just arrived from far away. What do people here take for granted? What do they hope for? What do they fear? Who is lonely? Don't judge it; just look. If you pray, you can hold your neighbors before God, one doorway at a time. The bell holds the time.
Newbigin's return. Lesslie Newbigin, home from India, seeing his own country as a mission field, and the local church as the place the gospel is explained by being lived.
Your line: home as mission. Today, take your usual route as if it were new, and notice one neighbor you've never really seen. Day one thousand two hundred eighty-one.

howItsDone: Some congregations speak of their own neighborhood as their mission field, through hospitality, local service and simply being present; Newbigin's books are read by church leaders across traditions.

Biography stated without dates: English-born minister of the Church of Scotland who served in India for years, learned Tamil, became a bishop in the Church of South India, and returned to Britain near the end of his working life. Confirm. 'Thinner congregations' is a soft description of what he found; confirm or cut.

Newbigin paraphrased (copyrighted): the West's unquestioned beliefs; Christians having made too much peace with them; the congregation as the 'hermeneutic of the gospel' (his phrase, used unquoted in the trapdoor). Newbigin wrote 'the only hermeneutic'; the superlative is dropped under the claims rule.
'This week has walked through a house of many rooms' echoes the year's title ('many rooms', from John 14:2); not quoted.

Original: πέμπω (John 20:21 has κἀγὼ πέμπω ὑμᾶς; the first verb, ἀπέσταλκεν, is from ἀποστέλλω). Confirm.
